Send In the Clones

Leapmotor, Omoda, Jaecoo and half the crossovers on any American freeway are turning into the same gray appliance. Maybe that's the point.

By Douglas James · 26 minute read

Leapmotor. Omoda. Chery's Jaecoo. Park them nose to nose in a parking lot, put a strip of painter's tape over every badge, and ask a stranger which one is which. Then ask a car person. I'll save you the trouble. They all look the same.

Same tall, rounded shoulders. Same roof sloping down into the same "floating" rear pillar. Same big wheels filling the same arches. Same tablet glued to the same dashboard. Same 4 paint colors, and none of them is actually a color.

And it isn't just them. Walk any mall parking lot in America and the crossovers in the $20,000 to $60,000 range are melting into one another like crayons left on a dashboard in July. You can tell a Toyota from a Kia from a Chevrolet if you know the tells, the way a sommelier can tell one Napa cabernet from another. Most people don't know the tells. Most people don't want to.

The person who put it best isn't a critic or a columnist. Anthony Lo spent years running design at Renault and now runs it at BAIC, one of China's biggest state carmakers. He told Fortune in late 2024 that there were so many new cars everywhere that I couldn't figure out which brands they belong to. That is a chief designer of a Chinese automaker saying it out loud, on the record.

And maybe that is the point.

The Art World Problem

People will not care. Only a select few will, and those are the enthusiasts.

Think of them as art lovers, or people in the art world. They see a painting or a sculpture and pay millions for something that looks ridiculous, or completely ordinary, to everyone outside that world. A blank canvas with one stripe down the middle. A banana duct-taped to a wall. To the insider, it's a conversation. To everyone else, it's a banana.

Cars work the same way. Show a non-car person the Mercedes-Benz 300 SLR Uhlenhaut Coupé and they will see a pretty old silver car. Show it to a car person and they'll tell you it sold for €135 million in 2022, about $143 million at the time and roughly $163 million in today's money, which makes it the most expensive car ever sold at auction. Same object. Two completely different worlds looking at it.

Here is where the analogy breaks, though. A painter answers to nobody. A car company answers to shareholders, and to the thousands of workers on its assembly lines whose mortgages depend on the thing selling. An automaker has a responsibility to make a profit, and profit lives in the middle of the market, not the edges.

The enthusiast cars are the ones the select few know about, want, and strive for. For everyone else, a car is just a means to get from point A to point B in comfort, with ease, in relaxation, possibly with some style, and with the least amount of effort for the best value, both up front and over the years of owning it. They just buy it and move on with their lives.

That's not me being a snob. That's the data. When YouGov asked Americans what matters most when choosing a car, price came first at 61%, reliability second at 51%, safety third at 31%. Style limped in at 15%.

And the art-world comparison turns out to be more literal than I expected. In 2005, psychologists Helmut Leder and Claus-Christian Carbon tested how people judge car interiors and found that participants with an interest in art were measurably more sensitive to the design differences than everyone else. The insiders really do see things the rest of us don't. A few years later, a team of marketing researchers sorted luxury buyers into "patricians," who want quiet signals only other insiders can read, and "parvenus" and "poseurs," who want the logo big enough to see from space. The enthusiast is the patrician. Everyone else is just trying to get to work.

Most shoppers don't even walk in knowing what they want. Cox Automotive's 2025 buyer study found 71% of new-car buyers started shopping "with an open mind." Only 29% knew exactly what they were after, down from 37% in 2020. That isn't a market of collectors. That's a market of people grabbing whatever is on the shelf that works.

Four Shades of Gray

Individuality isn't only leaving through the shape. Color has gone away.

The new-car market is now dominated by 4 shades: white, black, gray and silver. It's rare to see a car that is yellow, green or blue outside of a sports car, a Jeep Wrangler, a Ford Bronco or a high-end hypercar. You probably noticed this before you could put a number on it. Here is the number.

In the 1996 model year, 47.3% of the cars Americans drove were white, black, gray or silver, according to iSeeCars, which tracks millions of used-car sales by model year. By the 2025 model year that figure was 80.4%. Paint supplier Axalta counts new cars built worldwide a different way and lands in exactly the same place: 81% neutral in 2025. Yellow, by iSeeCars' count, is down to 0.1% of recent cars. One in a thousand.

It wasn't always like this. In the early 1990s, green was the color of America. PPG, one of the big paint makers, had green at 23% of North American cars in the mid-1990s, before it started to slip in 1997. Teal had its own following. Green Explorers, green Cherokees, green Tauruses, green everything. Gray, meanwhile, was a rounding error at 3.6%. Today gray alone is nearly 23% and green is barely 2%.

iSeeCars executive analyst Karl Brauer summed it up in 2024: Colorful cars appear to be an endangered species.

So why? Part of it is the dealer. Dealers stock what moves, and what moves is what doesn't scare anyone, so the lot fills up with gray and the buyer who walked in open-minded drives home in what was there. Part of it is the buyer's fear that a bright car will be hard to sell later. And part of it is simple economics at the factory: on many cars, the neutrals are the free paint. When Ford rolled out the 2024 Mustang, the only no-cost colors left were Carbonized Gray, Oxford White, Shadow Black and Iconic Silver. Race Red, Grabber Blue and the rest cost $295 extra, about $313 today. Even Dark Matter Gray ran $495, about $526 today. On the most expressive car Ford makes, the company charged you to have an opinion.

The menu has shrunk too. A 1973 Lincoln Continental could be ordered in 26 shades. The 2020 Continental offered 10, and half of those were grayscale.

The holdouts really are the toys. iSeeCars' segment numbers show sports cars as the last place color survives in any real quantity: 63.6% grayscale, against 79% to 84% for everything else. Jeep took orders for nearly 30,000 Wranglers in Tuscadero, a hot magenta, in the first 3 months it was offered in 2021. Ford has never published its Bronco color mix, but you have seen how many Cyber Orange and Area 51 Broncos are out there.

One correction to the theory, though, and it's an interesting one. Not every off-roader keeps its color. The least colorful vehicles in America right now are the big status SUVs: 98.6% of Toyota Land Cruisers, 97.5% of Lexus LXs and 99.1% of Cadillac Escalade IQs are white, black, gray or silver. The most colorful are the cars that are trying to make you smile, like the Volkswagen ID. Buzz and the Fiat 500e, each about 75% in a real color. Color has become the mark of a car that doesn't take itself seriously. Gray has become the uniform of money.

And here is the irony that should keep every gray-buying, resale-worrying shopper up at night. The safe colors are the expensive ones. iSeeCars tracked 1.2 million 3-year-old cars and found yellow lost 24.0% of its value, orange 24.4% and green 26.3%. Black lost 31.9%. White lost 32.1%. Brauer's explanation is simple supply and demand: nobody makes enough yellow cars, so the people who want one have to pay up for a used one. White and black give a used-car buyer nothing to fall in love with.

To be fair to the industry, the slide has stopped. iSeeCars says grayscale share has sat at about 80% since the 2020 model year, and BASF's latest paint data shows green as the fastest-growing color worldwide, cracking the top 3 non-neutral colors for the first time. The variety hasn't disappeared so much as moved into the finish. In North America, 17% of white cars now wear a pearl. Black comes in metallics, micas and tints you need a showroom light to see. It's color for the insiders again. The art world, in paint.

The Same Shape, Over and Over

The shapes are molding together too, and not just among the Chinese cars. The SUVs are all rounded, bubbled and curved, with similar styling and the same stance.

Start with the obvious: we stopped buying anything else. In 1975, 81% of the light vehicles built for America were sedans and wagons, and SUVs were 2%. By 2020, sedans were down to 31% and SUVs were 52%. Worldwide, SUVs were 48% of all cars sold in 2023, according to the International Energy Agency. When half the market is the same kind of box, you get a lot of boxes that look alike.

Then the box gets squeezed from every side.

Former Jaguar design director Ian Callum told Road & Track's Drew Magary, There was a time when you could identify the country the car came from. He went on to point out that trunk lids across the industry now land within about an inch of each other, because they're all shaped in the same wind tunnels chasing the same numbers. In an electric car those numbers are range. Stellantis design chief Ralph Gilles told Magary that a few counts of aerodynamic drag can be worth 10 miles of range. A designer who wants a sharper nose has to go explain to an engineer why the car should go 10 miles less.

Then come the safety rules, and these are rules nobody sensible would want repealed. Europe's pedestrian-protection standards, adopted in 2003, require enough room between a hood and the hard engine underneath to cushion a person's head, roughly 10 centimeters (4 inches) of it. Hoods went up. The European advocacy group Transport & Environment measured average new-car hood height rising from 76.9 centimeters (30.3 inches) in 2010 to 83.8 centimeters (33.0 inches) in 2024. In the US, the 2009 roof-crush rule doubled the load a roof has to carry before it gives, to 3 times the car's own weight. Roof pillars got fatter to do it. Taller fronts, thicker pillars, smaller windows: every car that meets those rules ends up wearing a version of the same suit.

Kia and Hyundai's longtime design boss Peter Schreyer said it plainly back in 2013, listing the engine, the 5 seats, the length, the headlight rules and the pedestrian rules every car has to meet. His conclusion: you really can't avoid similarities - it's impossible.

There was a time when you could identify the country the car came from.

Ian Callum, former Jaguar design director

Then there's the platform. Volkswagen's MQB architecture launched in 2012 and has since underpinned more than 40 million cars, around 70 models across 7 brands. Gasgoo, the Chinese auto-industry outlet, reports that about 70% of the components in a new Chinese car now come from generic modular platforms. When the bones are shared, the bodies built on top of them start to rhyme.

Someone has actually measured this. In 2015, 2 researchers, Corrado Costa and Jacopo Aguzzi, ran 3D shape analysis on 44 models from Fiat, Ford, Renault and Volkswagen across roughly 60 years. Their conclusion: European car shapes are converging toward one similar, compact, teardrop-like form, fastest of all in the smallest cars. It isn't your imagination. It has a peer-reviewed paper.

Did the Computer Do It?

Here's my theory, and I'll own that it is a theory. But the evidence is right in front of us.

Look at the cars of the 1920s and 1930s. They are gorgeous. Those endless hoods, those lines. The Duesenberg Model J debuted in 1928, and the bare chassis alone cost $8,500, about $165,000 in today's money, before a coachbuilder had even started on the body. Mercedes-Benz unveiled the supercharged 540K at the 1936 Paris show. The 1936 Cord 810 hid its headlights inside its fenders, the first production car to do it. Jaguar's XK120 arrived in 1948 as the fastest production car in the world and still looks like it was poured rather than built. Its successor, the 1961 E-Type, is the car Enzo Ferrari is said to have called the most beautiful ever made, and New York's Museum of Modern Art put one in its permanent collection in 1996.

Then the Cadillacs with their tail fins. Harley Earl, the father of American car design, said his mission was to lengthen and lower the American automobile, and by 1959 the Eldorado's fins had grown to the largest Cadillac would ever make them. Pure theater. Completely unnecessary. Absolutely wonderful.

Then the Ferraris from the 1950s through the 1970s. Ferrari built 36 250 GTOs between 1962 and 1964, and in the US one cost $18,000 new, about $199,000 today. One sold privately in 2018 for about $70 million. A shape, hand-hammered over a wooden buck, is now worth more than most office buildings.

Once computers became relevant and found their way into the designer's room, they started to cut the art and create similar shapes. That's exactly what a computer is programmed to do. A human isn't.

I went looking for the evidence, and the honest answer is more interesting than I expected.

The computer arrived much earlier than most of us think. General Motors switched on DAC-1, short for Design Augmented by Computer, at its Warren, Michigan, tech center in April 1963. Renault started UNISURF in 1968, the system built on Pierre Bézier's curves, the same curves still sitting inside every design program today. CATIA, the software that went on to shape roughly 4 in 10 new cars by the 1990s, spun out in 1981. If computers alone made cars look alike, the sameness should have started in the 1960s. It didn't.

When people first complained that every car looked the same, around 1983, they didn't blame the computer. They blamed the wind tunnel. The 1982 Audi 100 had just hit a drag coefficient of 0.30, a record for a production car, and suddenly everyone's car was a smooth jelly bean. The 1986 Ford Taurus followed. The aero look didn't come from software. It came from a fan the size of a house.

So the timeline doesn't convict the computer by itself. But the people who use them every day will tell you it isn't innocent either.

Frank Stephenson, who drew the modern MINI and worked at Ferrari, Maserati and McLaren, has argued that designers are losing the sensitivity that came from drawing by hand and shaping clay, and that you can see it in the cars. Of one electric car's geometric shape, he said: it's not design, it's algebra or trigonometry.

Marcello Gandini, the man who drew the Lamborghini Miura and Countach, put the problem somewhere else entirely, in the size of the room. Pointing to the Citroën DS, he said you can't have a collaboration among 100 or 200 people. A modern styling center has hundreds. Former BMW design chief Chris Bangle walked a rival's stand at the 2017 Frankfurt show and admitted, I can't find a new idea.

And the defense? Giorgetto Giugiaro, who designed the original Volkswagen Golf and the DeLorean, told Car Design News this year that the more rules there are, the smarter the product can be. You just have to think harder. BYD's design chief Wolfgang Egger says his team treats AI as a tool and keeps human intuition at the center. And full-size clay models are still being milled and hand-finished in nearly every carmaker's studio in the world.

When brands do risk-free design, they transfer the risk to the entire industry.

Shao Jingfeng, chief design expert, SAIC

So did the computer do it? Here's where I've landed. Partly, yes, just not the way the theory first sounds.

A computer doesn't draw one shape. A computer solves problems. Hand 50 design teams the exact same problem: a 1,975-kilogram (4,354-pound) box (the average new American vehicle, according to the EPA) that has to cushion a pedestrian's head, hold up 3 times its own weight on its roof, wring 10 more miles out of the wind, sit on a shared platform, reach showrooms in 18 months and offend absolutely nobody. Every one of those teams will hand back the same answer. The computer just gets them there faster, with fewer arguments. It isn't the robber. It's the getaway driver.

SAIC's chief design expert Shao Jingfeng, speaking about his own industry this August, called out the real crime: when brands do risk-free design, they transfer the risk to the entire industry. Optimization was always going to converge. That's what optimizing means. The art died when nobody was allowed to be wrong anymore.

The Toaster Theory

Cars are turning into appliances.

Think about the last time you bought a toaster. There's a paradox of choice with almost every appliance: 40 toasters, 30 washing machines, 25 refrigerators in stainless that all look identical under the store lights. At the end of the day you start not to care, because they all do the same job in roughly the same way. So you just get one.

"Paradox of choice" isn't just a figure of speech, either. It's the title of psychologist Barry Schwartz's 2004 book, and it comes from a famous experiment. In 2000, researchers Sheena Iyengar and Mark Lepper set up a jam-tasting table in a California grocery store. When it offered 24 jams, more shoppers stopped, but only 3% of them bought anything. When it offered 6, 30% bought.

I'll be honest about the asterisk, because this is where a lot of pop psychology gets it wrong. When researchers pooled 50 experiments on choice overload in 2010, the average effect came out at roughly zero. More choice doesn't always freeze people. But a bigger 2015 review, covering 99 results, found exactly when it does: when the choices are complicated, when the decision is hard, when you aren't sure what you prefer, and when you just want to get it over with.

Read that list again. That isn't a jam aisle. That's buying a car.

The other half of the psychology is the difference between maximizers and satisficers. The economist Herbert Simon coined "satisficing" in 1956: choosing what is good enough instead of hunting for the best. In 2002, Schwartz and his colleagues found that people who always chase the best possible option report less happiness, less satisfaction with what they buy, more regret and more depression than people who settle for good enough. The enthusiast is a maximizer by nature. I am a maximizer. I have spent more hours reading about one car than some people spend choosing a house. The appliance shopper has found the cheat code. You don't agonize over it.

And appliances often aren't chosen at all. They're replaced in a hurry. The Consumer Federation of America found half of refrigerator and washer replacements happened because the old one died. Nobody falls in love in that aisle. You need clean shirts by Thursday.

Now think about the brand on that appliance. You go into someone's home, see a toaster or a washing machine with a name you've never heard of, look it up, and find out the company is massive. That's Haier. In 2016 it bought GE Appliances for $5.6 billion, about $7.8 billion today, and market researcher Euromonitor has ranked it the world's number one major-appliance brand 16 years running. I'd bet most people with a GE fridge in the kitchen have never heard the name. They just know the fridge is cold.

The same thing is happening with cars, and it's happening fast. With the flood of new car companies coming to life, mostly if not all of them electric, people, even industry people, can't keep up. You see a badge, think "that must be a new company," and move on. In 2024, 129 different brands sold electrified cars in China, by consulting firm AlixPartners' count, and the firm expects only about 15 of them to still be viable by 2030.

Then look up the name you didn't recognize. Chery, Jaecoo's parent, sold 2.8 million cars in 2025 and has been China's largest car exporter for 23 straight years. Geely Holding sold 4.12 million, and its family includes Volvo, Polestar, Zeekr, Lotus and a big stake in Proton. SAIC sold 4.5 million and owns MG. Stellantis, the company behind Jeep, Ram and Dodge, paid €1.5 billion (about $1.6 billion then and $1.75 billion today) for a 21% stake in Leapmotor. The toaster with the weird name has a bigger factory than the toaster with the familiar one.

Getting Away From Status

And there's the genius in it.

When every car looks the same, nobody can tell what you paid. You are a number. And because no one can tell the difference, there's no shame and no shaming. Nobody is judging the crossover in the school pickup line. It gets people away from status, at least on the outside.

The research says status didn't die so much as go quiet. Sociologist Elizabeth Currid-Halkett has documented how wealthy Americans have shifted toward much more tacit signifiers of their social position, like spending on education, things you can't see from the curb. A study of 47 Mercedes-Benz models found that for every centimeter bigger the three-pointed star on the car, the price dropped by a little over $5,000 (about $7,600 today). The more you paid, the smaller the badge. Remember chart 6: the grayest vehicles in America are the Escalade, the Land Cruiser and the LX. Quiet money drives a gray truck.

The inside of the car is where the difference begins. Then again, some people don't care about that either. And in this day and age there's so much technology in even the most basic cars, big screens, driver assists, phone mirroring, heated everything, that the ultra-luxury brands really have to work to set themselves apart.

And not just in luxury, but in performance. You can buy a Genesis GV60 Magma, an electric crossover, for $69,950, and Genesis claims it will do 0 to 60 mph in 3.4 seconds. Bentley claims the same 3.4 seconds for the Bentayga Speed, at roughly 3.7 times the price. Not that anyone is cross-shopping the two. But the carrot that used to dangle in front of an exotic, beyond the presence, the status, the design and everything that goes with it, was performance. That carrot has been eaten.

Toyota's Akio Toyoda saw this coming back in 2017, worrying out loud that electric cars would become commodities, because once it is electrified, the acceleration is all the same. Pull up next to someone in an EV while you are sitting in an exotic or a sports car, and you no longer get to be smug about it, then take them off the line. In most cases you would lose.

I'm getting off topic.

But in fairness, status isn't gone for the people who want it. Back in 2003, J.D. Power found that cars with polarizing, love-it-or-hate-it styling sold about 4 days faster and earned about $609 more profit per car (roughly $1,100 today). As the firm's Chris Denove put it: It's better to polarize some shoppers than to generate mass apathy. Brave design still pays. It just pays the enthusiast, and the appliance car lets everyone else opt out of the game.

The Wave

And this is where the Chinese cars stop being a design story and become a business story. Lookalike design costs less. Much less.

Chinese automakers can take an all-new model from concept to showroom in as little as 18 months, according to Reuters. Western redesigns have traditionally come about every 5 years. The average Chinese-brand model on sale in China is 1.6 years old. The average foreign-brand model there is 5.4. Consulting firm AlixPartners estimates Chinese makers launch cars twice as fast, with 40% to 50% less investment. In the first half of 2026 alone, China launched more than 600 new or refreshed models. That's more than 3 a day.

Lo, the BAIC design chief, connected the two himself: development moves so fast, he told Fortune, that designers simply don't get the time to come up with all-new ideas, so they play it safe. Speed breeds sameness. Sameness is cheap. Cheap sells.

And it is selling everywhere. China passed Japan as the world's largest car exporter in 2023. It shipped 7.1 million vehicles abroad in 2025, and the industry's own trade group expects 10 million this year. Ford CEO Jim Farley came back from his trips to China and said it bluntly: It's the most humbling thing I have ever seen.

Chinese brands now take nearly half of new-car sales in Israel and Thailand, more than a third in Australia and Chile, about 1 in 6 in Mexico and 15% in the UK. Across Europe as a whole, they doubled their share in a single year, to 9.2% in the first half of 2026. Omoda only launched in Britain in late summer 2024, with Jaecoo following that winter, and the pair passed 100,000 UK sales in under 2 years. Leapmotor doubled its global deliveries in 2025 to almost 600,000, and this July it sold more than 100,000 cars in one month for the first time.

It isn't a straight line everywhere. Chinese brands' share in Russia has slipped from 54% to about 41% in a year, and in Turkey it dropped after new import duties. But on the map, one market stands out for being empty.

There are still no Chinese-brand cars for sale in the United States. A 100% tariff on Chinese-built electric cars has been in place since 2024, and a Commerce Department rule bars Chinese-controlled automakers from selling connected cars here starting with the 2027 model year, wherever they're built. (We broke that one down in Built Here, Banned Here.) In January and again in September, the President said publicly he would be fine with Chinese automakers building plants in America. In July, the Senate Commerce Committee unanimously advanced a bill that would cap Chinese ownership of automakers selling here at 15%. In September, 6 auto-industry trade groups asked the White House to keep Chinese automakers out entirely. Xi Jinping's state visit at the end of September extended the trade truce and produced no deal on cars. Next door, Canada agreed in January to let in up to 49,000 Chinese electric cars a year at a 6.1% tariff. For now, the clones are parked at the border.

The Pod

Follow the appliance idea all the way to the end and cars become really just transportation and nothing else for the masses. Maybe that's a good thing. They become self-driving pods that take you places safely and comfortably, without the stress.

Take Zoox. It's a brilliant design and concept, and it's in San Francisco right now. Amazon bought the company in 2020 for more than $1.2 billion, about $1.5 billion in today's money, and what it built doesn't look like a car at all. It's designed like a ski-resort gondola. If you've never ridden in one: the doors slide open like an elevator's, and you sit facing each other with tons of space inside. The San Francisco Standard's reporters called it a gondola-style interior after their first ride. The 4 seats face inward on 2 benches. There is no steering wheel. There are no pedals.

The clever part is that it never has to go in reverse. It's symmetrical, front and back, with steering on all 4 wheels, so once it parks, it simply drives forward again in the other direction. I guess if you want to get technical, it does go in reverse, depending on which direction you are facing. It tops out at 75 mph and carries a 133-kWh battery good for up to 16 hours of work.

Co-founder Jesse Levinson has said the goal was never to make a car drive itself. It was to make a new kind of transportation. That's the appliance theory taken to its logical conclusion. Nobody asks who made the elevator.

Or as former GM vice chairman Bob Lutz, the man behind the Dodge Viper, put it back in 2019: when you ride in the subway, do you care who made the subway car?

Zoox opened free public rides on the Las Vegas Strip in September 2025 and began charging for them on August 10 of this year. In San Francisco, riders from its public waitlist have been riding free since November 2025, and the service area quadrupled in March to take in the Marina, North Beach, Chinatown and the Embarcadero. Austin and Miami are next, and Zoox and Uber have announced that riders in Los Angeles will be able to book one through the Uber app in mid-2027. In July, federal regulators granted Zoox the first exemption of its kind, allowing up to 2,500 of the wheel-less vehicles a year to carry paying passengers. Its factory in Hayward, California, can build more than 10,000 a year once it is fully ramped. (We covered the regulatory side, and the robotaxi race, in The Meter, the App & the Machine.)

Pick Up and Go

So here's the theory, start to finish. The cars look the same because the rules, the wind, the platforms, the spreadsheets and the speed all push toward one answer, and the computer helps everyone arrive there at once. The colors are gone because gray is free, gray is stocked and gray offends nobody. The brands blur because China alone suddenly has 129 of them. And the masses don't care, because they never did. They wanted a toaster that works.

Pick up and go, just like grabbing a toaster or a pen. You don't agonize over it. You are a number. And because no one can tell the difference, no one can look down on you for it.

I used to think that was the sad part. I'm not so sure anymore. Every car that becomes an appliance makes the cars that aren't appliances mean more. When the parking lot was full of green Explorers and red Camrys, a yellow car was just a yellow car. When 4 out of 5 cars are white, black, gray or silver, the yellow one is louder than it has ever been. It's the 1 in 1,000. It's the painting in a room full of white walls. And according to iSeeCars, it'll even hold its value better.

The art world never needed everyone to care. It only needed the few who do.

So send in the clones. I'll be the one in yellow.
